title: Microprofile econ vs latency: annotated benchmark draft
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note is a working draft for a short collateral piece comparing latency vs unit-cost across a set of microprofiles we see in customer workloads. The goal is not to be exhaustive: it should produce crisp, shareable guidance for the Optimize UX and a one-page figure for sales/solutions. Focus: short-turn chat-like requests (prompt ~30 tokens, response ~40 tokens), mid-turn assistant completions (prompt ~120 tokens, response ~220 tokens), and long-form generation (prompt ~400 tokens, response ~1200 tokens).

Summary (top-level findings):
- For short-turn profiles, prefix/KV caching yields the single-largest latency improvement per dollar; warm cache + q8 dynamic-batching is the best tradeoff for p95-sensitive endpoints.
- For mid-turn workloads, modest batching (batch size 4–8) wins on cost with small p50/p95 penalties; heavy batching (>=16) reduces unit cost further but increases p99 by 2–4x in our traces.
- For long-form generation, quantization (q4f/q5x) reduces token cost significantly but may increase latency variance; if p99 is not critical, use q4f with opportunistic larger batches and prewarmed slots.

Methodology (short):
- Synthetic replay from production trace samples (anonymized) representing 10k requests per profile.
- Hardware: single A100-80GB equivalent node for all runs (isolated), kernel set X.
- Models: base-open-7B (FP16), base-open-7B-q8_1, base-open-7B-q4f.
- Configs evaluated:
  * Baseline: FP16, no cache, on-demand instances (cold start probability 8%).
  * Warm-KV: FP16 with KV cache primed from session history; cold start 1%.
  * Quantized: q8_1 and q4f variants with same cache setups.
  * Batching: no-batch, batch-4, batch-8, batch-16 (dynamic continuous batching).
  * Prewarm slots: reserved prewarm (affects cold start).
- Metrics: median latency (ms), p95 (ms), p99 (ms), tokens/sec (throughput), estimated unit cost ($ per 1M output tokens) using internal cost model (GPU utilization + infra overheads).

Workload microprofiles and representative request shapes:
- Short-turn (ST): 30 token prompt -> 40 token response. Tail-sensitive UI; p95/p99 matter.
- Mid-turn (MT): 120 -> 220 tokens. Balance latency and cost for conversational assistants.
- Long-form (LF): 400 -> 1200 tokens. Throughput-cost is primary; latency budgets are larger.

Annotated results (selected cells; numbers are medians over 3 runs):

1) Short-turn profile (ST) — median/p95/p99 latency and unit cost

Config                      | median | p95  | p99  | tok/s | $/1M out tokens
---------------------------|--------|------|------|-------|---------------
Baseline (FP16, no-cache)   | 210 ms | 520  | 980  | 240   | 9.8
Warm-KV (FP16)             | 120 ms | 260  | 420  | 410   | 8.1
q8_1 no-batch              | 150 ms | 340  | 640  | 320   | 6.6
q8_1 warm-KV               | 95 ms  | 210  | 360  | 520   | 5.7
q4f warm-KV batch-4        | 110 ms | 260  | 540  | 580   | 3.9
q4f warm-KV batch-16       | 170 ms | 520  |1200  | 1200  | 2.2

Annotations:
- Moving from Baseline -> Warm-KV reduces p95 by ~50% and median by ~43% at modest cost savings. This is the cheapest latency win for ST workloads.
- Quantization (q8_1) plus KV gives an additional ~28% median improvement and ~30% cost reduction versus FP16 warm-KV.
- q4f + aggressive batching yields best $/token but increases tail latency substantially; not acceptable for UI flows requiring p95 <300ms.

2) Mid-turn profile (MT)

Config                      | median | p95  | p99  | tok/s | $/1M out tokens
---------------------------|--------|------|------|-------|---------------
Baseline (FP16, no-cache)   | 420 ms | 980  | 1400 | 120   | 14.6
Warm-KV (FP16)             | 220 ms | 420  | 780  | 230   | 12.0
q8_1 batch-4               | 270 ms | 540  | 900  | 360   | 9.1
q8_1 batch-8               | 350 ms | 780  | 1500 | 630   | 6.4
q4f batch-8                | 320 ms | 840  | 2100 | 980   | 4.6
q4f batch-16, prewarm      | 420 ms | 1400 | 2800 | 1900  | 2.9

Annotations:
- For MT, batching to 4–8 gives sweet spot: ~30–45% unit cost reduction with small median increases. p99 grows more quickly — monitor if product requires low tail.
- q4f shows strong $/token wins for sustained workloads. Prewarming is important to keep perceived latency stable; without prewarm p99 is dominated by cold starts.

3) Long-form profile (LF) — generation throughput & cost

Config                      | median token-step (ms) | avg tok/s | $/1M out tokens
---------------------------|------------------------|----------|---------------
Baseline FP16              | 8.6 ms/token           | 116      | 18.4
q8_1 batch-16             | 5.2 ms/token           | 190      | 11.2
q4f batch-32 prewarm      | 3.6 ms/token           | 280      | 6.3
q4f batch-64 prewarm      | 2.9 ms/token           | 340      | 4.9

Annotations: long-form workloads benefit disproportionately from big batches and q4f quantization. If latency constraint is loose (p95 in multiple seconds acceptable), scale batch size aggressively for best unit economics.

Simple ASCII chart (cost vs median latency for sample configs, ST profile):

Cost ($/1M tokens)  | Latency median (ms)
--------------------|--------------------
  2  | ************************  (170 ms)
  4  | ***********************   (110 ms)
  6  | *****************         (95 ms)
  8  | ***********               (120 ms)
 10  | ******                    (210 ms)

(Shorter bar = lower cost; this crude chart shows q4f batch-16 at ~2$/1M but tail latency unacceptable for UI.)

Operational recommendations (practical):
- For customer-facing chat UI (ST): prefer FP16 or q8_1 with warm-KV and limit batch sizes to <=4; enable prewarm on high-SLA routes. Default recommendation: q8_1 + warm-KV + batch-4 if p95 <300ms is required.
- For assistant backends where a small additional latency is acceptable (MT): recommend q8_1 with batch=8 and prewarm; offer q4f as a cost-optimized tier behind feature flags.
- For long-form processing pipelines (LF): default to q4f + large batches + prewarmed reserved slots; accept higher latency variability.

Metrics and instrumentation to add to Console: 
- Per-route: p50/p95/p99 + token efficiency (tokens/sec normalized by model config).
- Cold-start heatmap: fraction of requests in last N minutes that experienced >100ms cold penalty.
- Cost delta explorer: compare $/1M between two config snapshots with same input trace.

Open questions and next steps (for the team):
- Re-run all configs on v2 kernel selector (patch in PR#482) — expected 5–12% latency improvement on q8_1.
- Explore hybrid mode: warm-KV + q8 runtime with selective q4f fallbacks for bulk generations. Needs workload routing experiments.
- Validate numbers on a multi-tenant cluster; single-node isolation understates noisy neighbor effects.
- Draft one-pager for sales that visually contrasts "fast UI" vs "low-cost batch" recommended stacks.

Appendix: raw-run notes and caveats:
- Cost model includes amortized infra (network, storage) and fixed per-slot overhead using current internal rates; absolute dollar numbers should be treated as relative signals not public pricing.
- Runs used a fixed-length tokenization assumption; real customer prompts with heavy system messages can change everything.
- p99 in q4f can be dominated by kernel-level dequant overheads on some request shapes; we flagged two GPU firmware variants during runs.

End of draft.

Notes to self: convert this to a one-page PDF with two annotated figures (ST scatter of cost vs p95 with recommended configs highlighted; LF throughput curve) before sharing with Solutions Eng on 2027-02-22 meeting.
